blocks.text: The ICP Museum in New York presents “I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now,” an exhibition organized by Aperture that brings together twenty-eight artists of different generations, from postwar Japan to the present day.
By Gaia Squarci. Cover photo by Asako Narahashi.

blocks.caption:
Ishiuchi Miyako, Mother’s #39, 2002. Courtesy Third
Gallery Aya, Osaka, and Aperture

blocks.text: The story of Japanese photography has mostly been told through men, though countless women helped shape it and remain largely overlooked. Curated by Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko, the exhibition grew out of Aperture’s 2024 book and its accompanying show at the Rencontres d’Arles. At ICP, the installations are as varied as the artists themselves. Three threads run through the work: close observation of everyday life, critical takes on the social roles Japanese women inhabit and reinvent, and experiments that push photography beyond its usual limits.

blocks.text: Asako Narahashi shoots from the surface of the water. Her images float between freedom and fear, as if the viewer could rise above the waves or sink beneath them at any moment. Miyako Ishiuchi’s Mother’s (2000–2005) unfolds as an intimate observation of the possessions her late mother left behind: lingerie, faded photographs, worn-down lipsticks. The series suggests that what we own may become the way we are remembered.

blocks.caption:
Yamazawa Eiko, What I Am Doing No. 77, 1986.
Courtesy Third Gallery Aya, Osaka, and Aperture

Yanagi Miwa, Elevator Girl House 1F, 1997; from the
series Elevator Girl. Courtesy the artist and Aperture

blocks.text: Hitomi Watanabe takes the visitor into the streets of Shinjuku, the heart of Tokyo’s 1960s counterculture. She photographed as an insider of the Zenkyoto student movement, which occupied the University of Tokyo campus in 1968–69 to demand academic reform and political change, and her images capture both the struggle and the everyday life of the protesters. These and many other bodies of work are a reminder that Japanese women photographers have been producing daring and intimate images for decades, largely outside the spotlight.
The exhibition “I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now” is on view at The International Center of Photography (ICP) in New York City until January 11, 2027.
